```
) -> (Vec<usize>, EarnStats) {
    let vtol = config.vertex_tolerance_mm;
    let stol = config.surface_tolerance_mm;
    let mut stats = EarnStats::default();

    let ladder = S::EARN_LADDER;
    let mut accepted = vec![seed];
    let Some(mut rung) = fit_rung(ladder[0], mesh, &accepted) else {
        stats.final_rung = "none";
        return (accepted, stats);
    };
    // Index into \`ladder\`, not a rung code: the loop only ever climbs toward
    // the type being earned for.
    let mut step = 0_usize;
    let mut last_refit = 1_usize;

    let mut seen: HashSet<usize> = HashSet::new();
    seen.insert(seed);
    let mut queue: std::collections::VecDeque<usize> = std::collections::VecDeque::new();
    let push_neighbours = |queue: &mut std::collections::VecDeque<usize>,
                           seen: &mut HashSet<usize>,
                           fi: usize| {
        let vc = mesh.faces[fi].vertex_count as usize;
        for &ni in &mesh.faces[fi].neighbors[..vc] {
            if ni < 0 {
                continue;
            }
            let ni = ni as usize;
            if in_region[ni] && seen.insert(ni) {
                queue.push_back(ni);
            }
        }
    };
    push_neighbours(&mut queue, &mut seen, seed);

    while let Some(cand) = queue.pop_front() {
        if rung.validates(mesh, cand, centroids, vtol, stol) {
            accepted.push(cand);
            push_neighbours(&mut queue, &mut seen, cand);
            // Refit on doubling; the current fit stays valid for what it has
            // already admitted either way.
            if accepted.len() >= last_refit * EARN_REFIT_GROWTH {
                if let Some(r) = fit_rung(ladder[step], mesh, &accepted) {
                    rung = r;
                }
                last_refit = accepted.len();
            }
            continue;
        }

        // The face does not validate. Try climbing the ladder: a higher rung
        // may explain the whole patch INCLUDING this face. Requiring every
        // already-accepted face to validate under the promoted fit is what
        // stops a promotion from quietly swapping in a surface that explains
        // the frontier at the cost of the patch.
        stats.promotions_attempted += 1;
        let mut trial = accepted.clone();
        trial.push(cand);
        let mut promoted = false;
        for next in (step + 1)..ladder.len() {
            let Some(r) = fit_rung(ladder[next], mesh, &trial) else {
                continue;
            };
            if trial
                .iter()
                .all(|&fi| r.validates(mesh, fi, centroids, vtol, stol))
            {
                rung = r;
                step = next;
                accepted = trial;
                last_refit = accepted.len();
                push_neighbours(&mut queue, &mut seen, cand);
                stats.promotions_accepted += 1;
                promoted = true;
                break;
            }
        }
        if !promoted {
            // Across a seam. Excluded, and recorded.
            stats.frontier_faces += 1;
        }
    }

    // One final refit, then drop anything it no longer explains, so the patch
    // that leaves here validates a single fit rather than a history of them.
    if let Some(r) = fit_rung(ladder[step], mesh, &accepted) {
        let kept: Vec<usize> = accepted
            .iter()
            .copied()
            .filter(|&fi| r.validates(mesh, fi, centroids, vtol, stol))
            .collect();
        if !kept.is_empty() && kept.contains(&seed) {
            accepted = kept;
            rung = r;
        }
    }
    stats.final_rung = rung.name();
    accepted.sort_unstable();
    accepted.dedup();
    (accepted, stats)
}
```

I'm mid-implementation on 1.2 with two long jobs running, so here's where it stands.

**Done so far** — the earn loop is written in [compete.rs](src/stage2/compete.rs):

- `earn_patch::<S>` grows a patch from the seed **face by face under validation**, admitting a frontier face only if it validates the current fit at `vtol` (the same `face_validates` bar the flood uses), climbing a per-type DOF ladder via the Phase 1.1 closed-form initializers as support accumulates, and excluding + counting faces that validate under no rung — the seam frontier Phase 2 consumes.
- Per-type ladders on the `SurfaceType` trait: plane `[0]`, sphere `[0,2]`, cone `[0,1,3]`, torus `[0,1,4]` — the plan's "plane → cylinder/cone or sphere → torus".
- Wired into `grow<S>` in place of `seed_patch`, bypassing `condition_patch` (kept for the other `grow_from` callers until 1.5's ablation), with counters behind `BREPPER_DEBUG_EARN`.

**One design correction I made mid-flight, worth flagging.** My first cut made the earned patch *type-agnostic* — one patch per seed, handed to every type. That's wrong, and it manufactures exactly the ambiguity the step's "branch on ambiguity" bullet proposes to branch out of: two adjacent facets of a sphere also validate a cylinder, so the ladder would climb to cylinder, grow a band, and hand `grow::<SphericalSurface>` a band-shaped patch — the under-determined case `MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG` exists to reject. Making the loop **type-directed** (each type earns its own patch, since the outer competition already enumerates types) removes the ambiguity at the source. So I have not implemented branching, and on this design I don't think it's needed — I'd rather show you the measurements than add a second model-selection mechanism alongside the competition that already exists.

**Two things I'm not yet sure of, both measurement questions:** whether `EARN_PATCH_CAP` (currently inherited from `SEED_PATCH_CAP` for cost only, not correctness) ever binds before the seam does, and what the NO-GROWTH count does against its baseline of 323 on stepped_block fine.

## 🤖💭 Assistant
<!-- msg_011CdbLgUnwnxUdCe5Rr2dyC -->

> The earn loop is causing failures that cluster around cone geometry and freeform surfaces like NURBS—I'm seeing issues across cone-sphere intersections, B-spline waves, elliptical arches, tangent plane calculations, and surface selection problems.
> 
> The core issue is that the ConicalSurface promotion ladder (plane → cylinder → cone) gets stuck on lower rungs. When a plane seed fails, it promotes to a cylinder, but a cylinder can approximate a cone locally well enough that it keeps accepting faces without ever needing to climb to the actual cone type. Since promotion only triggers on failure, and the cylinder approximation doesn't fail quickly, the loop never reaches the target geometry—it just keeps fitting thin bands of the cone as cylinder patches, which then either get rejected by sweep angle constraints or produce garbage when forced into a cone fit.
> 
> This is the same "wrong early rung poisons the patch" problem I identified with spheres, now manifesting in cones.
> 
> The solution is to flip the strategy: instead of climbing the ladder on failure, use the ladder purely to bootstrap enough support, then jump directly to the target type and stay there. For ConicalSurface, accumulate a minimum seed using the lowest rung, then fit the cone directly and validate under cone constraints only, never falling back to cylinder. Every accept should attempt promotion to the target rung, not just on failure—if it validates everything, switch immediately. This is a small but principled change: the patch should climb to its target type as soon as support exists. I'm also reconsidering whether promotion requires the target to validate all accepted faces, and I think it does. There's a concern about freeform and NURBS models that depend on analytic fits failing so leftovers fall back to B-splines—if the earn loop now produces different patches, those analytic fits might succeed when they shouldn't.
> 
> Let me fix the cone climbing first and re-run to see what clears. I'll restructure the accept branch to attempt climbing to the highest rung that fits and validates all accepted after each accept, rather than just trying the target on failure. The cost is fitting the target on every accept, which is O(k²) with k ≤ 32—about 1024 operations per seed per type, which is acceptable.
> 
> Restructuring the accept logic...
> 
> Before I commit to this, I should also check whether the earn loop is actually helping given the breakage we're seeing. I'll measure the NO-GROWTH and surface counts before and after on a couple of models to understand the direction, then implement the climb fix and re-run the full suite.

Fair — let me drop the jargon.

## What the cone fitter is handed

The earn loop starts at one facet and adds neighbours one at a time, keeping a face only if it lies on the surface it currently believes in. For a seed on the cone:

1. One facet on its own is just a plane, so that's the starting guess.
2. The next-door facet is tilted off that plane (the cone curves away), so the plane guess fails and the loop reaches for the next surface type up.
3. At that moment it has **three facets, all touching each other** — a patch a couple of millimetres across on a 30 mm cone.

Those three adjacent facets are what the cone fitter gets. In the traces it also retries at four, five and six facets as the patch inches along, and fails every time.

## Why that can't work

The fitter locates the cone's tip by intersecting the facets' planes — every facet of a cone is tangent along a line that runs to the tip, so all those planes should cross there.

That works when the planes arrive from genuinely different directions. But three facets sitting side by side on a cone are all tangent to nearly the same spot, so their planes are nearly the *same* plane, tilted a hair apart. Three nearly-parallel planes don't cross at a well-defined point — they graze each other along a long thin sliver, and a hair of error in any one of them slides the "tip" a long way. It's the same reason you can't find where three nearly-parallel lines cross: nudge one slightly and the crossing jumps across the room.

The measured result is exactly that failure: the tip lands halfway up the cone instead of at the point, and the cone comes out at 87° — almost a flat disc — instead of its true 18.4°. The fitter then checks that shape against the very three facets it was built from, none of them match, and the loop concludes "not a cone" and stops.

## Why cylinders don't have this problem

A cylinder's axis comes from crossing two facet normals, and that direction is exact even when the two facets are right next to each other — no spread required. So a cylinder is pinned down from the very first pair, which is why cylinders, spheres and tori all still come out byte-identical to before.

## What the old code did instead

`seed_patch` grabbed up to 32 nearby facets with similar curvature, without checking any of them. Thirty-two facets wrap a decent arc of the cone, so their planes really do arrive from different directions, and the fit is solid.

So the difference isn't the formula — it's how much of the cone the fitter can see. The blind patch showed it a swathe; the earn loop shows it a sliver, because it refuses to include a facet until it already has a surface good enough to judge it by. For a cone that's circular: it needs a wide patch to get a fit, and needs a fit to justify a wide patch.

The three ways out are still: keep the blind patch for cones only (everything else earned, and already verified unchanged); let the loop take one unchecked ring of neighbours first so it starts with a wider view; or make the cone fitter refuse to answer until its planes are spread enough to be trustworthy — which is honest but may just leave the cone stalled. I'd take the first and treat the cone as its own problem.

Yes — and I think that's the right diagnosis of the whole problem. The trouble isn't the fitting; it's that I chose a parameter that lives at infinity.

## Why the current parameters blow up

`(apex, axis, half-angle)` puts the apex — a point that can be arbitrarily far outside the data — at the centre of the estimate. A sliver of a cone has its apex far away, and the flatter the sliver the further away it goes, heading to infinity in the cylinder limit. Any estimator for a quantity that runs off to infinity as the data degenerates will explode near the degenerate case, which is exactly the 87°-and-apex-at-mid-height result.

It's the same reason nobody fits circles with radius `r`: a nearly straight arc has `r → ∞`. Circle fitters use curvature `κ = 1/r`, so the degenerate case is `κ = 0` — a finite, benign value sitting in the *middle* of the parameter range instead of at a singularity.

## The cone equivalent

Parameterize by local quantities and let the apex be derived:

- a point on the surface and its normal (both well determined by one facet),
- the **ruling direction** — the straight line the cone contains through that point,
- the **taper**: how fast the radius grows per unit length along the axis, i.e. `tan α`.

Taper is the cone's `κ`. A tiny patch gives taper ≈ 0, which is a *cylinder* — a completely valid, accurate description of a sliver of a cone, and precisely what the surface looks like locally. As the patch spreads the taper grows away from zero smoothly, and the apex gets computed once at the end, from `ρ₀ / tan α`. Nothing ever divides by a nearly-zero spread mid-loop.

Two things make this fit the ladder better than what I built:

1. **The cylinder stops being a separate rung** and becomes the `taper = 0` case of the cone. The plane → cylinder → cone jump becomes one continuous refinement, so there's no discrete promotion to fail.
2. **It reuses the exact construction that already works.** For a cylinder, crossing two adjacent facet normals gives the axis exactly (the 1.0 result). Working the same algebra for a cone gives `n₁ × n₂ ∝ cos α · d + sin α · r̂` — the **ruling direction**. So the one construction verified exact at minimal support hands you a ruling for free, in both cases; the cylinder is just where ruling and axis coincide.

## The honest caveat

The taper still has to come from somewhere, and on a three-facet patch it will be *uncertain* — but uncertain around zero, which is safe, rather than uncertain around infinity, which is not. The fit will explain its own three facets accurately either way (it's interpolating a short profile segment, not extrapolating to a far-off point), so validation passes and growth continues. That's the convergence behaviour you're asking about.

The residual risk is the axis direction, which the profile needs and which is genuinely poorly determined from a sliver. My instinct is that the fix is the same one: pick the minimum-taper solution consistent with the data, so the estimate leans toward "cylinder" until the evidence forces otherwise. But I'd want to measure that rather than assert it — it's the one part of this I haven't verified.

/// Phase 1.1 rejected a normal-covariance axis because the uncentred covariance
/// `Σ nnᵀ` has eigenvalues `cos²α/2` (twice) and `sin²α` (once), so the axis is
/// its smallest eigenvector only while α < 35.26°. **Centring removes that
/// regime entirely**, and the reason is short: on a cone
/// `nᵢ = cos α · r̂ᵢ − sin α · d`, so subtracting the mean normal cancels the
/// `sin α · d` term and leaves `cos α (r̂ᵢ − r̄)`, which lies in the plane
/// perpendicular to the axis **for every α**. The smallest eigenvector of the
/// centred covariance is therefore the axis exactly, at any half-angle, and the
/// 35.26° flip was an artefact of not centring.
///
/// What it does *not* fix is conditioning on a sliver: over a short arc the
/// `r̂ᵢ` are nearly collinear, so the centred normals span one direction rather
/// than two and the axis is pinned only to a plane — the meridian plane. The
/// remaining freedom within that plane is precisely the half-angle, which is
/// why [`cone`] resolves it by fitting a profile rather than by asking this for
/// more than it knows.
fn cone_axis_from_centred_normals(faces: &[usize], mesh: &ConnectedMesh) -> Option<[f64; 3]> {
    let mut normals = Vec::with_capacity(faces.len());
    for &fi in faces {
        if let Some(n) = mesh.faces[fi].normal {
            normals.push(n);
        }
    }
    if normals.len() < 2 {
        return None;
    }
    let inv = 1.0 / normals.len() as f64;
    let mut mean = [0.0_f64; 3];
    for n in &normals {
        for k in 0..3 {
            mean[k] += n[k] * inv;
        }
    }
    // Packing matches `build_normal_covariance`: [xx, xy, xz, yy, yz, zz].
    let mut cov = [0.0_f64; 6];
    for n in &normals {
        let c = [n[0] - mean[0], n[1] - mean[1], n[2] - mean[2]];
        cov[0] += c[0] * c[0];
        cov[1] += c[0] * c[1];
        cov[2] += c[0] * c[2];
        cov[3] += c[1] * c[1];
        cov[4] += c[1] * c[2];
        cov[5] += c[2] * c[2];
    }
    let mut axis = super::smallest_eigenvector_3x3(&cov);
    if normalize3(&mut axis) < MIN_CROSS_NORM {
        return None;
    }
    Some(axis)
}

/// A cone **or** a cylinder, in the taper parameterization.
///
/// # Why not (apex, axis, half-angle)
///
/// Phase 1.2 measured the cost of estimating the apex directly: on three
/// adjacent facets of an 18.4° cone the plane-concurrence solve returned a
/// half-angle of 87° with the apex halfway up the model, and the fit then
/// validated none of the three facets it was built from. The apex is a point
/// that runs off to **infinity** as a patch flattens toward a cylinder, and any
/// estimator for an unbounded quantity explodes near its degenerate case.
///
/// So this fits the *taper* — `dρ/dz`, the radius gained per unit length along
/// the axis — which is the cone's analogue of curvature. A circle fitter uses
/// `κ = 1/r` for exactly this reason: the degenerate case (a straight line)
/// becomes `κ = 0`, a finite value in the middle of the range, rather than
/// `r = ∞`. Here `taper = 0` is a **cylinder**, which is an accurate
/// description of a sliver of a cone rather than a failure to describe it.
///
/// The fit is a straight-line least squares through the patch's own
/// `(z, ρ)` profile, so it interpolates its support instead of extrapolating to
/// a far-off point. That is what makes it degrade gracefully: on a small patch
/// the slope is uncertain but the fit still explains every facet it was given,
/// so validation passes and the patch keeps growing; as the patch lengthens the
/// slope sharpens and the cone emerges on its own.
///
/// Returns a [`Initial::Cylinder`] when the taper is below what the patch can
/// resolve — `|t| · L ≤ vtol` over an axial extent `L` means the whole radius
/// change across the support is lost inside the tolerance the fit is validated
/// at, so the data does not distinguish it from a cylinder. That test is
/// derived from the tolerance and the patch geometry; it introduces no constant.
pub(crate) fn cone(faces: &[usize], mesh: &ConnectedMesh, vtol: f64) -> Option<Initial> {
    let mut axis = cone_axis_from_centred_normals(faces, mesh)?;

    let verts = patch_vertices(faces, mesh);
    if verts.len() < 3 {
        return None;
    }
    let inv = 1.0 / verts.len() as f64;
    let mut origin = [0.0_f64; 3];
    for &vi in &verts {
        let v = &mesh.vertices[vi];
        origin = add(origin, scale([v.x, v.y, v.z], inv));
    }

    // The (z, ρ) profile about the axis through the patch centroid.
    let profile = |axis: [f64; 3]| -> Vec<(f64, f64)> {
        verts
            .iter()
            .map(|&vi| {
                let v = &mesh.vertices[vi];
                let w = sub([v.x, v.y, v.z], origin);
                let z = dot3(&w, &axis);
                let radial = sub(w, scale(axis, z));
                (z, norm(radial))
            })
            .collect()
    };
    let mut pts = profile(axis);

    // Least-squares line ρ = a + t·z.
    let line = |pts: &[(f64, f64)]| -> Option<(f64, f64)> {
        let n = pts.len() as f64;
        let mz = pts.iter().map(|p| p.0).sum::<f64>() / n;
        let mr = pts.iter().map(|p| p.1).sum::<f64>() / n;
        let mut szz = 0.0;
        let mut szr = 0.0;
        for &(z, r) in pts {
            szz += (z - mz) * (z - mz);
            szr += (z - mz) * (r - mr);
        }
        if szz <= 0.0 {
            return None;
        }
        let t = szr / szz;
        Some((mr - t * mz, t))
    };
    let (mut a, mut t) = line(&pts)?;

    // Orient the axis so the radius grows along it; then the apex is behind.
    if t < 0.0 {
        axis = [-axis[0], -axis[1], -axis[2]];
        pts = profile(axis);
        let (a2, t2) = line(&pts)?;
        a = a2;
        t = t2;
    }

    let zmin = pts.iter().map(|p| p.0).fold(f64::MAX, f64::min);
    let zmax = pts.iter().map(|p| p.0).fold(f64::MIN, f64::max);
    let extent = zmax - zmin;
    let mean_radius = pts.iter().map(|p| p.1).sum::<f64>() / pts.len() as f64;

    // Below this the whole radius change across the support hides inside the
    // tolerance the fit is judged at: the patch cannot tell cone from cylinder,
    // and the cylinder is the honest answer.
    if !(t.is_finite() && t * extent > vtol) {
        if !(mean_radius > 0.0) {
            return None;
        }
        return Some(Initial::Cylinder {
            axis_pos: origin,
            axis_dir: axis,
            radius: mean_radius,
        });
    }

    let half_angle = t.atan();
    if !(half_angle > 0.0 && half_angle < std::f64::consts::FRAC_PI_2) {
        return None;
    }
    // The apex is where the fitted profile reaches zero radius — derived, and
    // never used while the patch is growing.
    let z_apex = -a / t;
    let apex = add(origin, scale(axis, z_apex));
    Some(Initial::Cone {
        apex,
        axis_dir: axis,
        half_angle,
    })
}

'''

///
/// Phase 1.2 measured the cost of estimating the apex directly: on three
/// adjacent facets of an 18.4° cone the plane-concurrence solve returned a
/// half-angle of 87° with the apex halfway up the model, and the fit then
/// validated none of the three facets it was built from. The apex runs off to
/// **infinity** as a patch flattens toward a cylinder, and an estimator for an
/// unbounded quantity explodes near its degenerate case.
///
/// So both shape parameters come from quantities that stay bounded and local,
/// and neither is derived from the apex:
///
/// * the **axis direction**, exactly, from the centred normal covariance;
/// * the **taper** `sin α = |n·d|`, averaged over the facets — a nearly
///   constant quantity on a cone, so averaging it is well conditioned however
///   short the patch is. (It carries the `O(Δθ²/8)` chord-plane bias Phase 1.1
///   measured — 1.5e-3 relative at Δθ = 0.11 rad — which is a rounding error
///   beside the failure it replaces, and shrinks as the mesh refines.)
///
/// Only the *position* then needs solving, and it is a plain linear least
/// squares. Writing `u` for the axis offset from the patch centroid within the
/// plane perpendicular to `d`, `z_A` for the apex's axial coordinate, and
/// `m = |u|² − tan²α · z_A²`, the surface condition
/// `|r − u|² = tan²α (z − z_A)²` rearranges to
///
/// ```text
///   |r|² − tan²α z² = 2 r·u − 2 tan²α z · z_A − m
/// ```
///
/// which is linear in `(u₁, u₂, z_A, m)`. Least squares then returns whatever
/// best explains the support, so the fit **interpolates its own facets** rather
/// than extrapolating to a far-off point — that is what makes it degrade
/// gracefully. On a short patch `z_A` is uncertain, but the residuals on the
/// data stay small, so validation passes and the patch keeps growing; as the
/// patch lengthens `z_A` sharpens and the cone emerges on its own.
///
/// `taper = 0` is a **cylinder**, a finite value in the middle of the parameter
/// range rather than `apex = ∞` at its edge — the same reason circle fitters
/// use `κ = 1/r`. A patch whose whole radius change hides inside `vtol` cannot
/// distinguish the two, and this returns the cylinder in that case. That test
/// is derived from the tolerance and the patch's own extent; it adds no
/// constant.
pub(crate) fn cone(faces: &[usize], mesh: &ConnectedMesh, vtol: f64) -> Option<Initial> {
    let mut axis = cone_axis_from_centred_normals(faces, mesh)?;

    // sin α from the normals: constant on a cone, so an average is stable at
    // any patch size, and it never touches a position.
    let mut sin_sum = 0.0;
    let mut count = 0_usize;
    for &fi in faces {
        if let Some(n) = mesh.faces[fi].normal {
            sin_sum += dot3(&n, &axis).abs();
            count += 1;
        }
    }
    if count == 0 {
        return None;
    }
    let sin_alpha = (sin_sum / count as f64).clamp(0.0, 1.0);
    let cos_alpha = (1.0 - sin_alpha * sin_alpha).max(0.0).sqrt();
    if cos_alpha <= MIN_CROSS_NORM {
        return None; // a plane, not a cone
    }
    let tan_alpha = sin_alpha / cos_alpha;

    let verts = patch_vertices(faces, mesh);
    if verts.len() < 4 {
        return None;
    }
    let inv = 1.0 / verts.len() as f64;
    let mut origin = [0.0_f64; 3];
    for &vi in &verts {
        let v = &mesh.vertices[vi];
        origin = add(origin, scale([v.x, v.y, v.z], inv));
    }
    let (e1, e2) = perpendicular_basis(&axis);

    // Axial extent decides whether the taper is resolvable at all.
    let mut zmin = f64::MAX;
    let mut zmax = f64::MIN;
    let mut mean_radius = 0.0;
    let local: Vec<(f64, f64, f64)> = verts
        .iter()
        .map(|&vi| {
            let v = &mesh.vertices[vi];
            let w = sub([v.x, v.y, v.z], origin);
            let z = dot3(&w, &axis);
            let r = sub(w, scale(axis, z));
            zmin = zmin.min(z);
            zmax = zmax.max(z);
            let (r1, r2) = (dot3(&r, &e1), dot3(&r, &e2));
            mean_radius += (r1 * r1 + r2 * r2).sqrt() * inv;
            (z, r1, r2)
        })
        .collect();

    // Below this the whole radius change across the support hides inside the
    // tolerance the fit is judged at: the patch cannot tell cone from cylinder,
    // and the cylinder is the honest answer.
    if tan_alpha * (zmax - zmin) <= vtol {
        let (axis_pos, radius) =
            super::cylindrical::fit_circle_for_axis(&axis, &verts, &mesh.vertices)?;
        return Some(Initial::Cylinder {
            axis_pos,
            axis_dir: axis,
            radius,
        });
    }

    // Linear least squares for (u1, u2, z_A, m).
    let t2 = tan_alpha * tan_alpha;
    let mut ata = nalgebra::Matrix4::<f64>::zeros();
    let mut atb = nalgebra::Vector4::<f64>::zeros();
    for &(z, r1, r2) in &local {
        let row = nalgebra::Vector4::new(2.0 * r1, 2.0 * r2, -2.0 * t2 * z, -1.0);
        let rhs = r1 * r1 + r2 * r2 - t2 * z * z;
        ata += row * row.transpose();
        atb += row * rhs;
    }
    let sol = ata.lu().solve(&atb)?;
    if !sol.iter().all(|v| v.is_finite()) {
        return None;
    }
    let (u1, u2, z_apex) = (sol[0], sol[1], sol[2]);

    let axis_point = add(origin, add(scale(e1, u1), scale(e2, u2)));
    let apex = add(axis_point, scale(axis, z_apex));

    // Orient the axis from the apex toward the support.
    let mid = 0.5 * (zmin + zmax);
    if mid < z_apex {
        axis = [-axis[0], -axis[1], -axis[2]];
    }
    let half_angle = tan_alpha.atan();
    if !(half_angle > 0.0 && half_angle < std::f64::consts::FRAC_PI_2 && mean_radius > 0.0) {
        return None;
    }
    Some(Initial::Cone {
        apex,
        axis_dir: axis,
        half_angle,
    })
}

'''

> At 3 facets, the fit error drops to 3.554e-3 mm, which is still well above the validation tolerance, so the loop continues to fail. The problem is that with only three nearly-collinear surface normals, the covariance matrix becomes poorly conditioned—the normals essentially span just one dimension, leaving the axis direction underconstrained to a plane. This means the entire coordinate frame built from that axis is misaligned, throwing off both the axial and radial position estimates.
> 
> The solution is to apply minimum-taper regularization: when the axis is ambiguous within that plane, choose the direction that minimizes the taper angle—which is the ruling direction of the cone, where the normal is perpendicular to the axis. This gives sin α = 0, effectively fitting a cylinder instead. An osculating cylinder to three adjacent cone facets should fit them quite well, staying close to the cone's natural deviation.
> 
> As the patch grows and the covariance becomes genuinely 2D, the true axis emerges and the taper becomes resolvable. Rather than relying on a threshold for the eigenvalue ratio, I can compute both the cylinder and cone fits and compare their residuals on the support—whichever explains the patch better wins. This data-driven approach naturally yields cylinders on slivers and cones on actual cones.
> 
> I'll implement a helper function to compute the maximum residual for a given fit against the vertices, then use that to pick the better model, with ties favoring the cylinder since it has fewer degrees of freedom.

s = s.replace("pub(crate) fn cone(faces: &[usize], mesh: &ConnectedMesh, vtol: f64) -> Option<Initial> {",
              "fn cone_tapered(faces: &[usize], mesh: &ConnectedMesh, vtol: f64) -> Option<Initial> {", 1)

wrapper = '''
/// A cone or a cylinder — whichever **explains the support better**.
///
/// The taper solve below needs the axis *direction*, and on a sliver that
/// direction is not determined: the centred normals span one direction rather
/// than two, so the axis is pinned only to the meridian plane and the remaining
/// freedom within it is exactly the half-angle. Measured, a 3-facet patch of an
/// 18.4° cone yields a taper fit that misses its own vertices by 3.6e-3 mm —
/// far better than the 87° the apex form produced, but still well above `vtol`,
/// so an earn loop would still starve on it.
///
/// The resolution needs no threshold on the ambiguity. Compute the cylinder
/// too — that construction is exact from two facets, and on a cone `n₁ × n₂`
/// gives the *ruling* direction, which is the minimum-taper member of exactly
/// the ambiguous family — then keep whichever candidate explains the patch
/// better. On a sliver the cylinder wins because the cone fit is numerically
/// adrift; once the patch spans enough arc for the axis to be determined, the
/// cone's extra freedom earns its place and it wins on residual. Ties go to the
/// cylinder, which has fewer parameters.
///
/// This is the same criterion the surrounding competition already uses —
/// explain the data — applied one level down, so it introduces no new kind of
/// decision.
pub(crate) fn cone(faces: &[usize], mesh: &ConnectedMesh, vtol: f64) -> Option<Initial> {
    let verts = patch_vertices(faces, mesh);
    let tapered = cone_tapered(faces, mesh, vtol);
    let straight = cylinder(faces, mesh);
    match (tapered, straight) {
        (Some(t), Some(c)) => {
            let (rt, rc) = (
                max_residual(&t, &verts, mesh),
                max_residual(&c, &verts, mesh),
            );
            Some(if rt < rc { t } else { c })
        }
        (Some(t), None) => Some(t),
        (None, c) => c,
    }
}

'''
s = s.replace("/// A cone **or** a cylinder, in the taper parameterization.", wrapper + "/// The taper solve itself: axis from the centred normals, half-angle from the\n/// normals, and only the position from a linear least squares.\n///\n/// # Why not (apex, axis, half-angle)", 1)
s = s.replace("""/// # Why not (apex, axis, half-angle)
///
/// # Why not (apex, axis, half-angle)""", "/// # Why not (apex, axis, half-angle)", 1)
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("ok")

   regime outright: on a cone n = cos(a) r - sin(a) d, so subtracting the mean
   normal cancels the sin(a) d term and leaves cos(a)(r - rbar), which lies in
   the plane perpendicular to the axis for EVERY half-angle. The 35.26 deg flip
   was an artefact of not centring, and the replacement is exact.

2. The parameterization. (apex, axis, half-angle) puts a point that runs off to
   infinity as the patch flattens toward a cylinder at the centre of the
   estimate, and any estimator for an unbounded quantity explodes near its
   degenerate case. Both shape parameters now come from bounded local

   facets — and only the POSITION is solved, as a plain linear least squares in

   the range rather than apex = infinity at its edge, the same reason circle
   fitters use kappa = 1/r. A patch whose whole radius change hides inside vtol
   returns the cylinder, a test derived from the tolerance and the patch's own
   extent rather than a constant.

Cylinder vs cone is then decided by which explains the support better, not by a
threshold on the ambiguity — the same criterion the surrounding competition

## 🤖 Assistant
<!-- msg_011CdbRe1LUPH9t2Jj6UCNcq -->

The taper reparameterization worked as theory but not as rescue. Here's the honest result.

## What the reparameterization fixed

Two genuine defects in the 1.1 cone initializer, now landed (`e931ea9`), suite **595 passed / 0 failed**:

1. **The 35.26° covariance flip was an artefact of not centring.** On a cone `n = cos α·r̂ − sin α·d`, so subtracting the mean normal cancels the `sin α·d` term exactly and leaves vectors lying in the plane perpendicular to the axis — *at every half-angle*. The centred covariance's smallest eigenvector is the axis, full stop. 1.1's whole "the covariance axis is only right below 35.26°" finding was me measuring an uncentred covariance.

2. **The apex explosion is gone.** Shape now comes only from bounded local quantities — axis from the centred normals, `sin α = |n·d|` averaged — and only the *position* is solved, as a plain linear least squares. `taper = 0` is a cylinder, a finite value mid-range, exactly as `κ = 1/r` makes a straight line finite for a circle fitter.

Measured on three adjacent facets of an 18.4° cone:

| parameterization | half-angle | validates its own 3 facets |
|---|---|---|
| (apex, axis, half-angle) | **87°**, apex mid-model | **0 of 3** |
| taper | correct sign, converging | worst residual **3.6e-3 mm** |

## Why it still doesn't rescue the earn loop

3.6e-3 mm is **70× the 5e-5 vertex tolerance** the loop validates at. So the cone still starves at two faces, and `cone_cylinder` still collapses (4 surfaces → 132). A hybrid — cone keeps the blind patch, other three earn — fixes the pure-cone models but leaves freeform and tangent-cone models failing.

The reason is now precise, and it isn't a parameterization problem any more: on a narrow patch **the axis direction and the half-angle trade off against each other inside the meridian plane**. The normals pin the plane but not the angle within it; separating them needs angular spread the sliver doesn't have. That's a joint nonlinear solve — which is exactly what the existing least-squares fitter does once it has a 32-face patch.

## The finding

The phase thesis is that closed-form initializers make a validated patch viable. They do — **but only where the closed form is exact at minimal support.** `n₁ × n₂` needs no angular spread, so cylinders (and spheres, tori) work: for those four types the earn loop reproduces the existing decomposition **byte-identically** (`rounded_cube_10_r2_fine` 26 = 6/12/0/8/0/0; `filleted_pipe` 8 = 2/2/0/0/4/0). The cone has no such construction.

So the blind patch was solving a real chicken-and-egg — a fit needs support, and in this design support needs a fit — and better formulas alone don't dissolve it. On this evidence **1.5's plan to delete `seed_patch` is premature**, which I've recorded.

## Where I left it

- Landed: the cone fix (`e931ea9`) and the 1.2 findings in TODO (`71e7a48`).
- Not landed: the earn loop. It's saved as a 1080-line patch in the scratchpad rather than committed, since it breaks the corpus.
- The pre-phase baseline sweep is still running; it's moot for these two commits, which are behaviour-neutral (`initialize.rs` is reachable only from tests), but it'll be needed before any real 1.2 attempt.

Three open routes, none decided: let the loop take a small unvalidated bootstrap (~1 ring, not 32 faces); grow the cone by a route that doesn't need its axis up front; or accept a per-type hybrid. I'd want your call before spending more on it — the second is the only one that preserves the phase's thesis intact, and it's also the least certain.

Faces 8 and 9 have **the same normal to 7 digits** — `(0.9407, 0.1293, 0.3136)`. Same θ, different height: they're on the **same ruling**.

A cone is developable, so its tangent plane is *constant along a ruling*. The earn loop starts with a plane, and BFS hands it the neighbour up the ruling — which lies in that plane to 5e-7, comfortably inside `vtol`. So it accepts it, stays on the plane rung, and walks up the ruling collecting coplanar facets.

Then it tries to go *around* the cone, where the real curvature is, and those faces are 0.03–0.6 mm away. Rejected. Promotion is attempted six times and fails every time — because the patch it's promoting from is a **flat strip with zero normal variation**. `n₁ × n₂ = 0`; the centred normal covariance is rank 0. No curved surface can be initialized from it, ever.

The first candidate is circumferential, it fails the plane, and promotion fires immediately with two genuinely different normals. The cone's rulings are subdivided into four bands, so there's a flat path to walk.

Not a bootstrap, and not identifiability gating — both of those were treating symptoms. The loop's **frontier ordering** is wrong. It takes BFS order, which on a developable surface preferentially eats the direction with zero curvature. It should prefer the candidate that most increases the patch's normal spread — which is exactly `|n₁ × n₂|`, the conditioning quantity Phase 1.0 already established governs everything here. That also predicts the cylinder result: with a spread-first frontier, a cylinder patch would grow circumferentially from the start, which is where its conditioning comes from.

## The four mechanisms, in the order they had to be fixed

**1. Frontier ordering (your prediction).** A cone is developable, so its tangent plane is *constant along a ruling*. BFS walked the ruling, accepting coplanar facets at ~5e-7 mm, and built a flat strip with zero normal variation — rank-0 covariance, `n₁ × n₂ = 0`, from which no curved surface can ever be initialized. Picking the candidate that most increases `max |n_cand × n_acc|` inverts that. **Necessary, and alone it changed nothing** — still 132 surfaces.

**2. Premature commitment.** With two normals the centred covariance is rank 1, so the cone is mathematically undeterminable and the *cylinder* rung takes the pair instead — wrong by the half-angle on a cone, so it rejects the third face and deadlocks at two. Fixed by collecting spread-first *without committing* until the target rung is determinable, then validating everything retroactively. I made the cone axis solve decline at rank 1 rather than return an arbitrary answer.

**3. A fallback masking that.** My `cone()` wrapper fell back to a cylinder whenever the taper solve declined — which handed the deferred loop a confident answer built on support that determines nothing. "Axis undeterminable" and "genuinely a cylinder" are different states and now return differently.

Only quantities read from *vertices*, which lie on the surface exactly, can reach that bar. So the closed form's job is to break the chicken-and-egg by handing least squares a patch it can trust — it was never going to be the final answer. Seeding the closed form and refining with the existing `fit_surface` is what actually fixed it.

## The hole, precisely

It's in the deferred-commitment phase I added an hour ago:

```rust
let Some(cand) = take_widest(&mut queue, &accepted, mesh) else { break };
accepted.push(cand);        // ← added WITHOUT validation
```

During deferral, faces are added unvalidated, chosen to **maximize** normal spread. Near a tangent junction, once the patch has grown a little, a face across the junction often has the highest spread of any candidate — so the loop *actively reaches for it*. Then either the mixed patch validates as some higher-DOF surface (spurious spheres), or it never validates and the seed yields nothing (fragmented fillets).

That's the straddling the phase design claims is impossible "by construction". My deferral broke that guarantee.

Why `rounded_cube_10_r2_fine` still passes: the fine Parasolid mesh has many facets per fillet, so seeds far from junctions exist and win on area. The coarse OCCT remesh has few facets per fillet — *every* facet is near a junction — so there's no clean seed. Which is Phase 0's finding again: coarse meshes and narrow features are where everything breaks.

## What I think this actually reveals

Two different selection problems were conflated, and each of us got one right:

- **Which faces to collect** — wants *similarity*: faces you're confident lie on the same surface. Curvature similarity is a decent proxy, which is what `seed_patch`'s jet filter does.
- **Which faces to initialize from** — wants *spread*: conditioning, per Phase 1.0's `perpendicularity / |n₁ × n₂|`.

The blind patch got the first right and the second wrong (it hands `grow_from` a jet-similar blob with no attention to conditioning). My earn loop got the second right and the first exactly backwards — spread-first is the worst possible collection rule, because "most different normal" is a description of a face on another surface.

The fix that follows is to stop using one rule for both: collect jet-similar (or simply validated-only, never unvalidated), and *within* the collection pick the widest pair to initialize from. That also removes the need for the unvalidated deferral, since the collection no longer has to reach for informative faces — it just has to not leave the surface.

Your "expand in multiple directions" is the other candidate, and it's what the plan's 1.2 actually specifies ("branch on ambiguity; false branches self-prune within ~2 faces"). I dismissed branching earlier as redundant with the outer type competition — that was wrong: it's needed for *direction* ambiguity, not type ambiguity, which is a different thing.

I'd try the collection/initialization split first, since it's smaller and the diagnosis points straight at it, and keep branching in reserve for whatever survives. Want me to?

/// component containing `seed`.
///
/// Connectivity matters: a fit may happen to explain a detached island on the
/// far side of a junction, and adopting it would reintroduce the straddling
/// this is here to prevent.
fn connected_validating(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    patch: &[usize],
    seed: usize,
    ok: impl Fn(usize) -> bool,
) -> Vec<usize> {
    let in_patch: HashSet<usize> = patch.iter().copied().collect();
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    let mut seen: HashSet<usize> = HashSet::new();
    let mut stack = vec![seed];
    seen.insert(seed);
    while let Some(fi) = stack.pop() {
        if !ok(fi) {
            continue;
        }
        out.push(fi);
        let vc = mesh.faces[fi].vertex_count as usize;
        for &ni in &mesh.faces[fi].neighbors[..vc] {
            if ni < 0 {
                continue;
            }
            let ni = ni as usize;
            if in_patch.contains(&ni) && seen.insert(ni) {
                stack.push(ni);
            }
        }
    }
    out.sort_unstable();
    out
}

Your concern was correct, it was measurably happening, and it's now fixed.

## The evidence, before and after

| model | old | earn loop (before) | earn loop (now) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rounded_cube_offset_occt_medium` | 26 = 6/**12 cyl**/8 sph | 38 = 6/**24 cyl**/8 sph | **26** ✓ |
| `cone_tangent_planes_occt_medium` | 7 = 4/1 cone/**0 sph** | 10 = 4/2 cone/**2 sph** | 9 |
| `rounded_cube_10_r2_fine` | 26 | 26 | **26** ✓ |

Every fillet cylinder had been splitting in two, and two spurious spheres had appeared on the tangent-cone model — your scenario almost exactly.

## What was wrong and what fixed it

The hole was that my deferred-commitment phase added faces **unvalidated**, selected to maximize normal spread. Near a tangent junction that rule *actively reaches across the seam*, because "most different normal" is a fair description of a face on the neighbouring surface. Three corrections, in order of how much each mattered:

1. **Collect by curvature, not by spread.** Curvature distinguishes surfaces; normal direction doesn't. Two facets on one cylinder share principal curvatures however differently they're oriented.
2. **Spread is still right for *initialization*** — Phase 1.0's `perpendicularity / |n₁ × n₂|` — but that belongs inside the initializers, not in the collector. Two different questions; conflating them was the bug.
3. **Trim toward the seed rather than giving up.** This turned out to be the largest single effect: when the seed failed its own patch's fit I was clearing the patch, and 747 of 762 earn calls returned a bare seed. Dropping the farthest face and retrying — `condition_patch`'s reasoning, that an unfittable collection is unfittable *because* its far end is on another surface — recovered everything.

Curvature alone isn't sufficient either, and the rounded cube shows why: the fillet radius and the corner-sphere radius are both 2, so curvature doesn't separate them. The trimming is what handles that.

**590 passed / 5 failed / 32 ignored** — same count as before, different set: `remesh_cone_tangent_{medium,fine,offset}`, `nurbs_bspline_hill_stage41_compare`, `freeform_models_decompose_rather_than_collapsing`. `cone_tangent_planes` went 7 → 9, so I've traded one junction failure for a smaller one.

## The meta-finding, which I think is now the real result of 1.2

The earn loop has converged, step by step, back to **`seed_patch` + `condition_patch`** plus a ladder choice and closed-form seeding. Every attempt to remove a piece of the blind machinery reintroduced a failure that piece was preventing:

- remove blind collection → cone starves (chicken-and-egg)
- collect by spread → straddles tangent junctions (your case)
- collect by curvature only → contaminated where curvature doesn't separate surfaces
- validate in one shot instead of trimming → 98% of seeds produce nothing

So **1.5's plan to delete `seed_patch`, `condition_patch`, `PATCH_TRIM_ROUNDS` and the rest is wrong on this evidence** — they're load-bearing, and the four fragility cliffs attributed to them are the price of a real problem rather than of arbitrary tuning. That's worth writing into the plan regardless of whether the earn loop lands.

Uncommitted; saved as a 674-line patch. I've stopped short of committing because it's still 5 tests short of green and I'd rather you see the shape of the result than have me keep grinding — the last four rounds each cost hours and each surfaced a mechanism I hadn't predicted.

# Surface Fitting Algorithms

This document describes the surface fitting math and validation algorithms used in brepper's Stage 2 pipeline. Each section covers the fitting math and validation for one surface type.

> **Orientation (post stage-2 rewrite).** The per-type **fitting math and
> validation** below (the \`fit_surface\`/\`vertex_distance\`/convexity content)
> is current — those fitters now implement the trimmed \`surface::SurfaceType\`
> trait and are driven generically by the whole-region DOF ladder
> (\`classify.rs\`) and scoped competition (\`compete.rs\`). The **BFS region
> growing / seeding / acceptance-test / seeding-mask** orchestration this
> document still refers to in places was the old pipeline and **no longer
> exists** (removed in Rewrite Roadmap step 7); read those mentions as
> historical. See [DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md](DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md) §2 for the
> current partition-then-classify architecture.

---

## General Approach

"Region growing" from seed faces while preserving fit invariants, refitting as necessary as faces are added to the region. Given that vertices lie within epsilon of precisely on the surfaces involved, any seed on a surface should grow to the entire region. The generic BFS algorithm is described in [DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md](DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md#generic-bfs-hypothesis-generation).

---

## 2.1 Planar fitting math

**Plane fitting** uses **area-weighted normal averaging**: each face's unit normal is weighted by the face's triangle area, then the weighted sum is normalized. The plane distance is the mean of \`normal · vertex\` over all vertices in the hypothesis. This gives larger faces more influence on the plane orientation, which is more robust than unweighted averaging.

- With the \`--compare\` flag:
  - For each hypothesis, compute the centroid of each member face.
  - Project each centroid onto the fitted plane (perpendicular projection).

## Precision and conditioning (measured 2026-07-28)

What limits a fit is not the fitter but the data and the support. Three facts,
all measured on the corpus, that the fitting math has to respect.

**The accuracy floor is a float32 quantum, and it scales with the model.** The
corpus ships *binary* STLs, so vertices are float32 and the floor on vertex
accuracy is \`max|coordinate| × 1.19e-7\`: 2.76e-6 mm for rounded_cube (max coord
23.1, measured stage-1 vertex distance 1.9e-6) and **1.96e-5 mm for
stepped_block_toroidal** (max coord 164, measured 1.23e-5). So "a mesh vertex
lies on the true CAD surface to ~1e-6 mm" is *not* a constant — it is twenty
times worse on a 164 mm part than on a 23 mm one, and a part exported 200 mm
off-origin carries ~10× worse data than one centred. Nothing downstream recovers
it. Expressed in quanta, committed analytic fits land at 0.3–0.5 (median) across
a 7× range of quanta, which is a scale-free way to say "as well as the data
allows".

**A short arc cannot determine a free surface of revolution, by any method.**
For an arc of half-angle θ on radius r the sagitta is ≈ rθ²/2. Over three
2.5° strips (7.5° of arc) on r = 0.5 that is ~0.001 mm against a 2e-5 mm
quantum, so the radius comes out ~2% wrong — 0.01 mm, or 200× vertex tolerance.
No fitting method repairs this; only more arc does. This is why an initial fit
taken from a small patch cannot be trusted, and why growth criteria must not
depend on the fit already being accurate.

**Constraining the axis collapses the problem.** Measured on the three fillet
cylinders \`stepped_block_toroidal\` fine fails to find: fixing *only the axis
direction* and fitting a 2D circle in the perpendicular plane recovers
**r = 0.99998, 0.99999 and 0.50008** (true 1.0, 1.0, 0.5) from arcs of 65°, 60°
and 40°, with maximum residuals of 1.0e-5, 1.0e-5 and 5.0e-6 mm — five to ten
times *under* vertex tolerance. The free 5-DOF fit fails on the **axis**, not the
radius. An adjacent committed surface supplies exactly that constraint (see
\`locus.rs\` and DEVELOPMENT_PLAN, "Rewriting stage 2.3(b)").

**Corollary for identifiability.** Residual cannot police over-parameterised
fits: the three spurious tori on that model fit their 7–8 faces to 0.52/0.72/0.87
quanta against genuine surfaces at mean 0.39, max 0.56 — overlapping, because a
7-DOF torus on 7 faces is essentially exactly determined. Guards must ask whether
the support *pins* the parameters (angular sweep, conditioning), never how small
the residual is.

---
=== Gaussian map section ===
### Gaussian Map (Normal Covariance) Classification

The distribution of surface normals (the "Gaussian map") directly reveals the surface type. For a patch of mesh faces, compute the area-weighted covariance matrix of the normals:
$$C = \sum_i w_i (n_i - \bar{n})(n_i - \bar{n})^T$$
where $w_i$ is face area and $\bar{n}$ is the weighted mean normal. The eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \lambda_3$ classify the surface:

- **Plane**: $\lambda_1 \approx \lambda_2 \approx \lambda_3 \approx 0$ — all normals identical.
- **Cylinder/Cone**: $\lambda_1 \approx \lambda_2 \gg \lambda_3$ — normals lie on a great circle (cylinder) or small circle (cone).
- **Sphere**: $\lambda_1 \approx \lambda_2 \approx \lambda_3$ (all nonzero) — normals distributed isotropically.
- **Torus**: $\lambda_1 > \lambda_2 \gg \lambda_3$ — normals form a band pattern.

The cylinder axis estimation already uses this: the axis is the eigenvector of the uncentered normal covariance $M = \sum w_i n_i n_i^T$ corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue (the direction perpendicular to all normals). Extending this to pre-classify surface type before fitting would improve seeding efficiency.

### Medial Axis / Tube Center Method

For any surface with a constant principal curvature $\kappa_1 = 1/r$ in one direction, the **medial axis** (locus of centers of curvature) can be computed directly from the surface points and normals:
$$k_i = p_i + r \cdot n_i$$

The geometry of the medial axis reveals the surface type:
- **Cylinder**: medial axis is a line (the cylinder axis) — $k_i$ points are collinear.
- **Sphere**: medial axis is a point (the center) — $k_i$ points cluster.
- **Torus**: medial axis is a circle (the major circle) — $k_i$ points lie on a circle.
- **Cone**: medial axis is a point (the apex) for one direction of curvature.

This is used in stage 2.4 (torus fitting): estimate $r$ from normal-line intersections between adjacent faces, compute tube centers $k_i$, fit a 3D circle to get the major circle, and extract the torus parameters.

p = "SURFACE_FITTING.md"; s = open(p).read()
anchor = "## Algorithm Reference"
new = r'''## Closed-form initialization from facet normals (measured 2026-07-31)

`src/stage2/initialize.rs`. Each analytic type fitted from a handful of facets
with no iteration, exploiting the fact that **facet normals carry exact
information** where a free least-squares fit on tiny support does not (see
"A short arc cannot determine a free surface of revolution" above). Unit-tested
to machine precision on synthetic strips. Not currently called by the pipeline.

### The constructions

- **Cylinder** — axis $= n_1 \times n_2$, exact from two facets and needing no
  angular spread at all; then radius and position from the existing
  `fit_circle_for_axis` over the patch's vertices.
- **Sphere** — the line through a facet's **circumcenter** along its normal
  passes exactly through the centre (the circumcenter is equidistant from three
  points of the sphere, so it lies on the axis of their circle). Two facets give
  the centre as the common-perpendicular midpoint; the radius is the mean vertex
  distance. The *centroid* does not have this property — only the circumcenter.
- **Cone** — see below; this one is not a single construction.
- **Torus** — the "bilinear" meridian-coplanarity system is **linear in Plücker
  coordinates**. With the axis line's moment $m = a \times d$ and
  $q_i = p_i \times n_i$, the constraint $(p_i - a)\cdot(n_i \times d) = 0$
  becomes $q_i \cdot d + n_i \cdot m = 0$ — one linear equation per facet in six
  unknowns, solved as a null space with no alternation and no starting guess.
  Geometrically it is just "every normal line of a surface of revolution meets
  the axis". The system must be normalized to the patch centroid and extent
  first: the $q$ block carries length units and the $n$ block does not, so on a
  patch far from the origin the null space drowns in the scale mismatch. Then
  $(R, r)$ from the existing `fit_circle_2d` on the $(\rho, z)$ profile.

### Why the cone needs a different parameterization

$(\text{apex}, \text{axis}, \text{half-angle})$ puts a point that runs off to
**infinity** as a patch flattens toward a cylinder at the centre of the estimate,
and any estimator for an unbounded quantity explodes near its degenerate case.
Measured on three adjacent facets of an 18.4° cone it returned a half-angle of
**87°** with the apex halfway up the model, and then validated **none** of the
three facets it had been built from.

Parameterize by the **taper** $dρ/dz = \tan\alpha$ instead — the cone's analogue
of curvature. `taper = 0` is a *cylinder*: a finite value in the middle of the
range rather than `apex = ∞` at its edge, exactly the reason circle fitters use
$\kappa = 1/r$ rather than $r$. Both shape parameters then come from bounded
local quantities — axis from the centred normal covariance, $\sin\alpha =
\overline{|n\cdot d|}$ — and only the *position* is solved, as a linear least
squares in $(u_1, u_2, z_A, m)$ from
$|r|^2 - \tan^2\!\alpha\,z^2 = 2r\cdot u - 2\tan^2\!\alpha\,z\,z_A - m$.

Two routes that do **not** work for a cone, both measured:

- **Normal-line concurrence** (the torus construction) is rank-deficient on a
  cone, and the degenerate case is what a real cone tessellation *is*: a cone is
  ruled, so one row of quads spans its whole height, every facet centroid sits at
  the same axial position, and their normal lines then all meet the axis at the
  **same point**. Any line through that point solves the system. On a torus the
  meeting point slides with the tube angle, which is why the identical solve is
  well posed there. "Surface of revolution" is not the enabling property —
  *variation in where the normal lines cross the axis* is.
- **Uncentred normal covariance** flips above 35.26° — see the Gaussian-map
  section.

### The limit of all of it: normals are chord planes

A facet's plane is a **chord** plane, not the tangent plane. For a strip quad
spanning two rulings the lean works out to
$n\cdot d = \sin\alpha\,\cos(\Delta\theta/2)/\sqrt{1 - \sin^2\!\alpha\sin^2(\Delta\theta/2)}$,
an $O(\Delta\theta^2/8)$ bias — predicted 1.5e-3 relative at
$\Delta\theta = 0.11$ rad and measured as 9.985° against a true 10.000°.

That bias is small against a *wrong answer* but large against a *tolerance*: at a
15.65° tessellation step it is 0.93%, roughly **200× the vertex tolerance**
fits are validated at. So a closed form built on facet normals cannot reach the
validation bar on a real mesh. Only quantities read from **vertices** — which lie
on the surface exactly — can. The practical rule:

> Take directions from normals, magnitudes from vertices, and treat a
> normal-derived shape parameter as a **seed for least squares**, never as the
> answer.

### Ruling alignment: when a facet normal is exact at all

A facet normal on a ruled surface is perpendicular to the axis **iff two of its
vertices share a ruling**. Project the vertices along the axis: they land on a
circle, the facet's plane is parallel to the axis iff those projections are
collinear, and three points on a circle are collinear only when two coincide.
So a triangle straddling three rulings tilts its normal off perpendicular
however perfect the underlying surface is.

Measured over the corpus's 12 cylinder-bearing models, 12 275 cylinder facets:
facets with an edge on a ruling are perpendicular to a worst case of
**0.0006°**, while the **25.6%** that straddle reach **1.0528°** — and every
non-zero perpendicularity in the corpus comes from a straddling facet. Quad
fusion is a 23× discriminator but not a guarantee (2.7% of fused quads straddle
against 62.3% of triangles).

**Tapering surfaces make alignment impossible in places.** A mesher holding
chord length roughly constant drops circumferential divisions as the radius
shrinks: `cone_cylinder` runs 32 divisions at its base ring, 23 through the
middle, 29 where the cylinder starts. Where consecutive rings disagree, *no*
facet can be ruling-aligned — no two vertices share a $\theta$ — and the strip
cannot fuse into quads. Where they agree, the facets fuse and their normals
agree to 7 digits.

### Conditioning: the amplification law

The axis error from a two-facet construction is
**$\text{perpendicularity error} / |n_1 \times n_2|$**, verified to 0.1% on
`pipe_elbow_10` Parasolid medium (a perpendicularity max of 0.0280° over a
conditioning p50 of 0.0271 predicts 1.033°; measured 1.0342°, constant across
all 348 pairs).

Adjacent facets differ in normal by the exporter's angular step, so
$|n_1 \times n_2| \approx \sin(\text{step})$ — p50 0.0432 on a fine mesh, which
is $\sin(2.48°)$ and independently recovers Onshape's 2.5° setting. **The
amplification is therefore ~23× on a fine mesh and gets worse as the mesh
refines**, which inverts the natural assumption that denser meshes fit better.
Pair the angularly *most distant* facets, never neighbours. A 90° reading is the
fully degenerate pair of two facets on one ruling strip: no information, rather
than a wrong answer.

**Selection is not collection.** Spread is the right rule for choosing which
facets to *initialize from*; it is the wrong rule for choosing which faces to
*collect*, because "most different normal" also describes a face on the
neighbouring surface. Collecting by spread split every fillet of
`rounded_cube_offset_occt_medium` (12 cylinders → 24) and invented two spheres on
`cone_tangent_planes_occt_medium`. Curvature distinguishes surfaces; normal
direction does not — but curvature is not sufficient either, since a rounded
cube's fillet radius equals its corner-sphere radius. See DEVELOPMENT_PLAN,
"Phase 1.2 as attempted".

---

''' + anchor
assert anchor in s
s = s.replace(anchor, new, 1)
open(p,"w").write(s)
print("SURFACE_FITTING updated")

Close out Phase 1.2: the blind patch is load-bearing, and why

Phase 1.2 set out to replace seed_patch + condition_patch with a patch grown
under validation. It was implemented, measured over five rounds, and NOT landed;
the code is preserved on branch phase-1.2-earn-loop-attempt (2b098d8), 5 tests
short of green. The result revises the phase rather than reporting a bug, so it
is written into all three documents.

Every attempt to remove a piece of the blind machinery reintroduced a failure
that piece was preventing:

* validated-only growth starves cones — a fit needs support, support needs a fit
* breadth-first collection walks the RULING, where a developable's tangent plane
  is constant, and builds a flat strip of rank-0 normals from which no curved
  surface can ever be initialized
* collecting by normal spread straddles tangent junctions: 12 fillets -> 24 on
  rounded_cube_offset_occt_medium, two spurious spheres on
  cone_tangent_planes_occt_medium. Which faces to COLLECT wants similarity;
  which faces to INITIALIZE FROM wants spread. Conflating them was the bug.
* collecting by curvature alone is contaminated where curvature does not
  separate surfaces — a rounded cube's fillet radius equals its sphere radius
* validating in one pass instead of trimming cost 747 of 762 earn calls

The best-performing form is seed_patch + condition_patch with a ladder choice
added: it converged back onto what it set out to replace. So Phase 1.5's
deletion list is not supported — those constants are the price of the
fit/support chicken-and-egg, not of arbitrary tuning.

Second consequence: closed-form initializers SEED least squares, they do not
replace it. sin(alpha) read from facet normals inherits the O(dtheta^2/8)
chord-plane bias — 0.93% at a 15.65 deg step, ~200x the tolerance fits are
validated at. Only quantities read from vertices reach that bar.

Also landed here, from the initializer work 1.2 forced: the cone axis declines
when the centred normal covariance is rank 1 (a patch along one ruling has
identical normals, so any axis would be arbitrary), and initialize::cone no
longer falls back to a cylinder when the axis was undeterminable — those are
different states and conflating them hands a caller a confident answer built on
support that determines nothing.

Docs brought to current state: TODO gets the Phase 1 status header, the refreshed
193-model baseline (113 ok / 78 fail / 2 timeout), and two new rule-6 dead ends;
DEVELOPMENT_PLAN gets "Phase 1.2 as attempted"; SURFACE_FITTING gets a
closed-form initialization section (the four constructions, the taper
parameterization, ruling alignment, the amplification law) and a correction to
its Gaussian-map section — the uncentred normal covariance flips above 35.26 deg
and centring removes the regime entirely.

Suite 595 passed / 0 failed / 32 ignored; clippy clean.

## What landed

**Code** — the two initializer fixes the 1.2 attempt forced out, both live and unit-tested: the cone axis now declines when the centred normal covariance is rank 1 (a patch grown along one ruling has identical normals, so any axis would be arbitrary), and `initialize::cone` no longer falls back to a cylinder when the axis was *undeterminable* — those are different states, and conflating them hands a caller a confident answer built on support that determines nothing.

**The earn loop itself** is on branch `phase-1.2-earn-loop-attempt` (`2b098d8`), 5 tests short of green, with a commit message saying so. It's in git history rather than a scratch file, and out of the main line so the pivot starts clean.

## Documents

**TODO** — Phase 1 now carries a status header saying 1.0/1.1 landed, 1.2 did not, and **1.3/1.4/1.5 should not be started as written**. The baseline is refreshed to the real current figure (193 models: 113 ok / 78 fail / 2 timeout — the corpus had grown past the recorded 158). Rule 6 gained two dead ends that both look obviously right: collecting a patch by normal spread, and validated-only growth.

**DEVELOPMENT_PLAN** — a "Phase 1.2 as attempted" section giving the five rounds and what each measured.

**SURFACE_FITTING** — this was the most out of date, last touched 2026-07-29. It now has a closed-form initialization section (the four constructions, the taper parameterization and why the apex form explodes, ruling alignment, the amplification law), a corrected orientation note, and a correction to its own Gaussian-map section: it claimed the axis is the smallest eigenvector of the **uncentred** normal covariance, which flips above 35.26° — a 90° countersink is 45°, and the corpus's `cone_15x20` is 36.87°. Centring removes the regime entirely.

## The finding worth carrying into the pivot

Every attempt to remove a piece of the blind machinery reintroduced a failure that piece was preventing, and the design converged back onto `seed_patch` + `condition_patch` with a ladder choice bolted on. Two consequences:

1. **1.5's deletion list is contradicted.** Those constants are the price of a real chicken-and-egg between fit and support, not of arbitrary tuning — so the four fragility cliffs attributed to them aren't free to remove.
2. **Closed-form initializers seed least squares; they don't replace it.** Anything read from facet normals inherits the chord-plane bias — ~200× the validation tolerance at a typical tessellation step. Only vertex-derived quantities reach that bar.

And the one that came directly out of your question, which I'd want any redesign to start from: **collection wants similarity, initialization wants spread.** They're different questions, and the blind patch and the earn loop each had exactly one of them right.
